Define optical flow, distinguish it from the motion field, and contrast it with stereo.
risposta: Optical flow is the apparent motion of brightness patterns between two frames from the same camera at different times - a 2D vector field of per-pixel displacements, used to infer object velocity or camera motion. The motion field is the true 2D projection of actual 3D scene motion; optical flow only approximates it and they can differ (a rotating uniform Lambertian sphere has motion field but zero flow; a static specular sphere under a moving light has zero motion field but nonzero flow). Stereo instead uses two cameras at the same time from different viewpoints for depth, where epipolar constraints reduce correspondence search to 1D; optical flow is an unconstrained 2D search.

domanda: Derive the optical flow constraint equation, explain the assumptions, and why it is underconstrained (the aperture problem).
risposta: Assumptions: brightness constancy (a point's intensity stays constant over time), small motion, and spatial coherence (neighbors move similarly). Brightness constancy gives I(x,y,t)=I(x+u*dt,y+v*dt,t+dt). A first-order Taylor expansion and cancellation yields the optical flow constraint Ix*u+Iy*v+It=0, where Ix,Iy are spatial gradients and It the temporal gradient. This is one equation with two unknowns (u,v), so it is underconstrained: solutions lie on a line in (u,v) space and only the flow component along the gradient (perpendicular to an edge) is determined - the aperture problem.

domanda: Explain the Lucas-Kanade method, when it works, and how coarse-to-fine handles large motions.
risposta: Lucas-Kanade adds spatial coherence: assume constant flow in an NxN patch, giving N^2 equations for two unknowns - an overdetermined system Ax=b solved by least squares, x=(A^T A)^{-1} A^T b. Here A^T A is the same second-moment matrix as in Harris; the solution is reliable when A^T A is invertible and well-conditioned (both eigenvalues large), i.e. in corner/textured regions. It fails in flat regions (eigenvalues small) and along edges (one eigenvalue near zero - the aperture problem). Large motions violate the small-motion assumption and are handled coarse-to-fine: build Gaussian pyramids, estimate flow at the coarsest level where motion is small, upsample and warp the next frame toward the first, compute residual flow, accumulate, and repeat down to full resolution.

domanda: Explain the Horn-Schunck method, including its energy functional and the oversmoothing problem with robust regularization as a remedy.
risposta: Horn-Schunck assumes the flow is smooth across the whole image and minimizes an energy with a data term enforcing brightness constancy (integral of (Ix*u+Iy*v+It)^2) plus a smoothness term penalizing large flow variations (lambda * integral of ||grad u||^2+||grad v||^2), where lambda controls regularization strength. The quadratic penalty implicitly assumes Gaussian noise and is not robust to outliers, so it penalizes large flow changes too heavily and oversmooths across object boundaries. The remedy is robust regularization: replace quadratic penalties with robust loss functions that are less sensitive to large errors, allowing sharp flow discontinuities at boundaries while still smoothing elsewhere.
